Baby & Child

When handwriting gets in the way of schoolwork

Updated: November 17, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Your child tells a lively story about a lost dog. On paper, only the first sentence is finished when the lesson ends. Ask them to read it back and show you where writing became hard work. The story they can tell and the marks they can put on the page give you different information.

Notice which part of writing is hard

Look at a short sample with your child. Can they form the letters they want? Do words run together or drift away from the line? Does the pencil leave deep grooves, or are the marks hard to see? Ask whether their hand tires or hurts. Note whether the difficulty appears while copying, writing their own ideas or both.

Children learn at different rates and in different scripts. Compare the work with what their teacher has taught. Letter formation, spacing, speed and putting ideas into words are related but separate skills. A hard-to-read page cannot tell you that a child is careless or diagnose dysgraphia or developmental coordination disorder.

Try one change on a real piece of writing

Support the child's feet and forearms, angle the page comfortably and use the other hand to steady it. A grip that is comfortable and works need not look the same as someone else's. With the teacher, choose one feature to practise in a short, useful task, such as spacing the words on a lunch note. Let the child pick the word that is easiest to read and show you what helped.

In a small study of children aged six to eleven with handwriting difficulties, groups practising handwriting or doing sensorimotor activities met four times a week for five weeks. The handwriting-practice group improved its handwriting, while the sensorimotor group did not. It does not set a home practice schedule for every child. Drawing can be enjoyable, but include the kind of writing the child actually wants to do.

Keep handwriting from hiding what they know

Bring the teacher a sample written at a comfortable pace and one from a timed task. Ask what happens in class and whether less copying, extra time, typing or dictating a longer answer would let the child show their ideas. Agree on one change and when to review it. Praise a specific gain, such as a word the child can now read back independently.

If writing remains painful, very tiring or persistently limits schoolwork despite support, speak with the child's clinician and school. An occupational therapist can assess how writing and other everyday tasks are going. Report loss of a previously established skill promptly. A child with sudden or rapidly worsening weakness in the face, arm or leg needs immediate medical assessment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Look at a short writing sample together and ask how the hand feels.

Agree with the teacher on one practical adjustment and a review date.

Seek assessment for persistent pain or functional difficulty, and promptly report loss of a skill. Sudden or rapidly worsening face or limb weakness needs immediate medical assessment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests keeping one note the child is pleased with. Bring it to the teacher alongside a harder example and ask what made the difference.

When to seek help

Stop a task that hurts. Seek advice for persistent pain or fatigue that limits writing, and promptly report loss of an established skill. Seek immediate medical assessment for sudden or rapidly worsening face, arm or leg weakness.

Evidence notes updated: November 17, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Describe letter formation, spacing, speed and comfort separately.
  • Practise one goal in a meaningful task and notice the child's own progress.
  • Ask the school how the child can show what they know while handwriting develops.

Frequently asked questions

What can we do at home?

Ask the teacher how letters are being taught. Try one short note, list or label using the same approach. Check seating, paper position and comfort, then stop before frustration or pain builds.

How can handwriting difficulty affect a child?

A child may struggle to finish timed work or read back what they wrote. Being corrected in front of classmates can hurt confidence. Ask what helps them show their ideas.

Why might my child's handwriting be hard to read?

They may still be learning letter forms, spacing or how to coordinate the pencil and paper. Working quickly or composing a difficult sentence can add demands. A sample alone does not identify the cause.

Why take the difficulty seriously?

Slow or effortful writing can limit participation even when the child understands the lesson. School support and, if needed, an assessment can identify ways to help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
